title: The widow's two mites (Mark 12:18–44)
hook: the great commandment, then a widow gives everything she has

segments.voice: Yesterday, render to Caesar: the coin carries Caesar's face, and every person carries God's image. Your line was you bear his image. Whose face did you see differently? Today, still in the Temple, two tiny coins. Day two hundred twenty-three.

The collection basket comes down the row at Mass. Some people drop in an envelope. Some tap their phone. A kid puts in a quarter his mom handed him. Nobody's watching. Or so we hope. Today, somebody is. Jesus is still in the Temple, still being questioned. Then the questions stop, and he sits down across from the treasury, where people drop their offerings into the collection chests, and he just watches. Rich people put in large amounts. And then a poor widow walks up with two tiny coins.
screen: `THE COLLECTION BASKET.` → `HE SITS AND WATCHES.` → `A WIDOW WITH TWO TINY COINS.`

segments.voice: First, the greatest commandment. Before the widow, a scribe asks Jesus which commandment is first of all. Jesus answers with the Shema, words Jews still pray today. In the Douay-Rheims: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God." Love him with your whole heart, soul, mind and strength. And the second: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." The scribe agrees, and Jesus tells him: "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God." In Mark, it's a warm moment between Jesus and a scribe. Second, a warning. Right after, Jesus warns about scribes who love long robes and the best seats, and who devour the houses of widows. Hold on to that word, widows. Third, the widow. She drops in "two mites, which make a farthing." Mites were lepta, tiny copper coins. Jesus calls his disciples over: "this poor widow hath cast in more than all they who have cast into the treasury." The rich gave from what they had left over. She, out of her want, "cast in all she had, even her whole living." Fourth, two ways to hear it. The traditional reading hears praise: whole-heart love, lived out with two coins, the commandment in action. Some readers also hear a lament, since the story sits right after the warning about those who devour widows' houses: a system that takes a poor woman's last coins. The two readings can stand together: the widow is honored, and those who would take from her are warned. Either way, Jesus measures her gift by what it cost her, not by the amount.
screen: `THE SHEMA: LOVE WITH YOUR WHOLE HEART.` · `BEWARE THOSE WHO DEVOUR WIDOWS' HOUSES.` · `TWO MITES, MORE THAN ALL.` · `MEASURED BY COST, NOT AMOUNT.` · then, large: `SHE OF HER WANT CAST IN ALL SHE HAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something small that costs. Settle and breathe. Ask yourself: what would be a two-coin gift for me today? Not a big donation. Something small that you'll actually feel. Your lunch hour, for someone who needs to talk. The last of the good coffee. A few dollars you were saving for yourself. An apology that costs your pride. Pick one. Picture giving it. Notice the little pinch. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
The widow's two mites. Two tiny coins, and Jesus says she gave more than all the rich, because she gave all she had. Today's word.
Your line: all she had. Today, give your small costly thing, and don't tell anyone how much it cost you. Day two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics give at the offertory of the Mass and through almsgiving, one of the three traditional practices of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and the Church teaches special care for widows and the poor.

original.note: Greek: two lepta, small copper coins. the old English is mites.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice story about giving generously.
what it means: a gift measured by its cost, not its size, right after the command to love God with everything.
what a scholar hears: two lepta making a quadrans, placed right after a warning about those who devour widows' houses.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 12:29, 12:31, 12:34, 12:42–44 given from memory; confirm wording.
The Sadducees' question (12:18–27) is not retold, only the section's second half; confirm acceptable.
The 'lament' reading (e.g. Addison Wright, 1982) is presented as what 'some readers also hear', beside the traditional praise reading; confirm balance.
Lepta as the smallest coins in circulation; two lepta = one quadrans ('farthing'): confirm.
The Shema is described as prayed by faithful Jews 'then and now': a neighbor reference only, not comparative.

Editor review: hook no longer opens 'Think of'; cut 'the least money in circulation' / 'the smallest coins there were' (hook, teach, word, match, original note), 'every faithful Jew', 'a rare warm moment', 'most Christians' and 'the Church has usually held both'; the narrator's 'God measures the gift' is now what Jesus says (12:43–44); 'religious leaders' now 'scribes', as Mark 12:38 has it.
